reason: The quote is verbatim from L.B. de Silva J.'s judgment and matches the headnote holding that unjust enrichment has no application where improvements are made for the owner's benefit; this was the ratio for setting aside the compensation award.

The holding and quote are accurate, but the court construed section 41 of the Public Trustee Ordinance (Cap. 88), whereas the tag SRC001-s2 points to the Prevention of Frauds Ordinance, so the statute is wrong.
The court adopted the quoted Nathan passage as the governing standard and it forms the basis of the headnote holding on want of reasonable and probable cause in malicious prosecution.
The quote is the verbatim headnote holding of a Full Bench that a Kandyan woman under twenty-one does not attain majority by marriage; no statute claimed.
The rule is accurate ratio, but section 80 is of the Courts Ordinance No. 1 of 1889 (as the statement itself says), not the Civil Procedure Code that SRC030 denotes, so the statute is mis-tagged.
The quote is the verbatim headnote holding and reflects the ratio that a person whose interest accrued before the court order is not a privy in estate for res judicata; no statute claimed.
The court held parol evidence admissible under section 98 of the Evidence Ordinance (SRC029) to show the meaning of the vilasam and remitted on that basis; quote and statute both check out.

The statement drops two material qualifications the court relied on: the gift must be of all or the greater part of the donor's property (or a thing of very great value), and the right is lost if the donor expressly renounced it.

The supporting quote is taken from counsel's submission (Peri Sunderam) rather than the court, and section 83 is of the Fiscal's Ordinance No. 4 of 1867, not the Matrimonial Rights and Inheritance Ordinance that SRC004 denotes.

The quote is a reproduction of In re Coomaraswamy discussing that case's different facts (mortgages/otty bond), the proposition is applied cited precedent rather than this case's own ratio, and the court construed the Stamp Ordinance No. 22 of 1909, not the Prevention of Frauds Ordinance (SRC001).

The statement of the rule is correct ratio, but the supporting quote is merely the deed clause being construed and does not itself articulate or support the legal rule; the actual reasoning sentence was not quoted.
The proposition is expressly labelled 'semble' obiter; Pereira J. said 'as at present advised' and left the question open, dismissing the appeal as premature, so it is not a decided rule.

The supporting quote is a passage from Velupillai v. Arumugam quoted in the judgment addressing the section 547 bar on suing without letters of administration, not the administrator's entitlement to the whole chose-in-action; section 547 CPC is not the statute grounding this rule.
